summary: Defines a DHCPv6 option that a Dual-Stack Lite B4 element uses to discover the IPv6 address of its corresponding AFTR, the Address Family Transition Router.

plainLanguage.summary: Dual-Stack Lite gives a home router IPv4 connectivity over an IPv6-only line by carrying IPv4 packets inside IPv6. To do that, the router has to know the address of the provider's tunnel endpoint at the other end. This RFC adds one DHCPv6 option that carries the name of that endpoint, so the router learns it the same way it learns every other setting: by asking the network for configuration.

questions: what is the dhcpv6 aftr name option
how does a b4 find its aftr
subtitle: A single DHCPv6 option that tells a Dual-Stack Lite home gateway where the provider's tunnel endpoint is.

tldr.problem: A Dual-Stack Lite home gateway cannot offer IPv4 connectivity until it knows where the provider's tunnel endpoint is. The network does not tell the gateway that Dual-Stack Lite is available, and the gateway cannot learn that endpoint address on its own.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a single DHCPv6 option, code 64, that carries the fully qualified domain name of the Address Family Transition Router. The gateway resolves that name with DNS to get an IPv6 address and uses it as the far end of its IPv4-over-IPv6 tunnel.
tldr.outcome: A gateway can be set up by the ordinary DHCPv6 exchange, with no extra configuration file. How the tunnel itself is established is left out of scope.

facts.label: Option fields
facts.value: option-code, option-len and a variable-length name

facts.label: Tunnels per interface
facts.value: At most one at a time

today: RFC 6334 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2011, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It defines one option code, 64, which identifies the AFTR name in a DHCPv6 exchange.

sections.title: Why the Gateway Needs the Endpoint Name
sections.content:
Dual-Stack Lite, described in RFC 6333, is a way of offering both IPv4 and IPv6 connectivity to customers who are addressed only with an IPv6 prefix, so no IPv4 address is assigned to the attachment device. One of its key components is an IPv4-over-IPv6 tunnel, commonly called a softwire.

A Dual-Stack Lite B4 device, the Basic Bridging BroadBand element at the customer end, has two gaps in its knowledge. It does not know whether the network it is attached to offers Dual-Stack Lite service at all, and even if it did, it would not know the remote endpoint of the tunnel it would have to set up.

The RFC closes the second gap with a DNS hostname, the fully qualified domain name of the Address Family Transition Router (AFTR), which is the provider-side end of the tunnel. Once that information has been conveyed, the presence of the configuration also tells a host to start Dual-Stack Lite service and become a softwire initiator. The conveyance itself uses a single DHCPv6 option that expresses the AFTR's domain name to the B4 element. How the B4 then establishes the IPv4-in-IPv6 softwire to the AFTR is out of scope for this document.
sections.plainLanguage:
Dual-Stack Lite lets a home router offer IPv4 over an IPv6-only line by putting IPv4 packets inside IPv6 packets. The router cannot do that until it knows the address of the provider's machine at the other end of the tunnel, and nothing in the network tells it.

This RFC passes that address over as a name, in the same kind of message a router already uses to get its address and its DNS server. The router then looks the name up with DNS to get the address it needs.

sections.title: The AFTR-Name Option
sections.content:
The option has the option-code and option-len fields that every DHCPv6 option has, followed by a variable-length tunnel-endpoint-name field holding a fully qualified domain name that refers to the AFTR to which the client MAY connect. The option code is 64, and it SHOULD NOT appear in any DHCPv6 message other than Solicit, Advertise, Request, Renew, Rebind, Information-Request and Reply.

The name field follows the encoding required by DHCPv6 (RFC 3315) Section 8: a single octet giving the length of one DNS label, at most 63 octets, followed by the label contents, repeated for each label until the name is exhausted, including a terminating zero-length label. The RFC's own example carries the name aftr.example.com., which is 18 octets long, so the option-len value would be 18.

An implementation validates the option by confirming six conditions: the option-len is greater than 3, the option-len is less than or equal to the number of octets remaining in the DHCPv6 packet, the individual label lengths do not exceed the option length, the name is of the valid format described in DHCPv6 Section 8, there are no compression tags, and there is at least one label of non-zero length.
sections.plainLanguage:
The option is short: a two-octet code, a two-octet length, and then the name of the provider's tunnel endpoint written in the encoding DHCPv6 uses for domain names, where each part of the name is preceded by its length.

Before using the name, the router checks six things: that the length field is plausible, that it fits inside the rest of the packet, that the parts of the name fit inside that length, that the encoding is the expected one, that nothing has been compressed, and that the name has at least one part with content.

sections.title: What the DHCPv6 Server Does
sections.content:
A DHCPv6 server SHOULD NOT send more than one AFTR-Name option, and SHOULD NOT permit the configuration of multiple names within one AFTR-Name option. Both of these conditions are handled as exceptions by the client, so an operator using software that does not perform these validations should be careful not to configure multiple domain names.

DHCPv6 clients and servers negotiate configuration values with the Option Request option, as described in Section 17.2.2 of RFC 3315. The consequence for this option is that a server will not reply with an AFTR-Name option if the client has not explicitly enumerated it in its Option Request option.
sections.plainLanguage:
The server is told to send at most one of these options and to put at most one name in it. If the software does not enforce that, the operator has to be careful, because the client will use only the first name it finds and ignore the rest.

The server also waits to be asked. A client has to list option 64 in its request for options, otherwise the server leaves it out of the reply.

sections.title: What the Client Does
sections.content:
A client that supports the B4 functionality of Dual-Stack Lite and conforms to this specification MUST include OPTION_AFTR_NAME in its Option Request option. Because the client needs a DNS name for address resolution, it MAY also include the OPTION_DNS_SERVERS option (RFC 3646). If it receives the AFTR-Name option, it MUST verify the option contents as described in Section 3.

The RFC refers to the B4 element and the DHCPv6 client together as the B4 system, because in different environments they may be integrated, joined, or separated by a third piece of software. If the B4 system receives more than one AFTR-Name option, it MUST use only the first instance. If the option contains more than one fully qualified domain name, distinguished by the presence of multiple root labels, it MUST use only the first name listed.

The B4 system then performs standard DNS resolution of the given name to resolve an AAAA Resource Record, as defined in RFC 3596. If any DNS response contains more than one IPv6 address, the B4 system picks only one and uses it as the remote tunnel endpoint for the interface being configured in the current message exchange. It MUST NOT establish more than one Dual-Stack Lite tunnel at the same time per interface.

A B4 system may have several network interfaces, and each may be configured differently: some may be attached to networks that call for Dual-Stack Lite and some to networks using normal dual stack or other means. The RFC therefore asks that the specification be applied interface by interface. If a B4 system is attached to several networks that provide the AFTR-Name option, it MUST configure a tunnel for each interface separately, because each Dual-Stack Lite tunnel provides IPv4 connectivity for a distinct interface. The means of binding an AFTR-Name and the tunnel configuration to a given interface in a multi-interface device are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage:
The client asks for the option by name, so the server knows it wants one, and it may ask for the DNS server addresses in the same request. When the option arrives, the client checks it before using it.

The client keeps the first name it receives and ignores any others, then looks that name up with DNS to get an IPv6 address. If the lookup returns more than one address, it takes one of them and uses it as the far end of the tunnel. It runs only one tunnel per interface.

A router with several interfaces handles each one separately, because a Dual-Stack Lite tunnel carries IPv4 for one interface only.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC presents no new security issues, but as with all DHCPv6-derived configuration state, it is possible that the configuration is being delivered by a third party, acting as a man in the middle. There is therefore no basis for trusting the access level represented by the Dual-Stack Lite softwire connection, and Dual-Stack Lite should not bypass any security mechanisms such as IP firewalls.

DHCPv6-related security issues are discussed in RFC 3315, and Dual-Stack Lite-related security issues are discussed in RFC 6333.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no new security rules. It does repeat the standing warning about DHCPv6: because anyone on the path can change the configuration, the tunnel that results cannot be treated as a trustworthy link, and Dual-Stack Lite must not be used to get around firewalls or other protections.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has allocated a single DHCPv6 option code, 64, referencing this document, delineating OPTION_AFTR_NAME.
sections.plainLanguage: The option has one number in the DHCPv6 registry: 64, which is reserved for the AFTR name.
